hints.title: Require both parts of a counterexample
hints.body: The function must first be integer-valued at every integer input. Its derivative must then fail to be integer-valued at at least one integer input. Test the functions at 0 and 1 to eliminate ineligible choices.
hints.recap: A counterexample has a true hypothesis and a false conclusion.
hints.pitfall: A non-integer value of f itself fails the hypothesis and cannot refute the implication.
hints.pause: Which options fail the hypothesis already at 0 or 1?

recall.reminder: Check every hypothesis before using a proposed counterexample.

hints.title: Test derivative integrality
hints.body: Differentiate each candidate still eligible after the first checks, then evaluate the derivatives at simple integers.
hints.recap: One non-integer derivative value refutes the derivative’s universal condition.
hints.pitfall: A derivative exception alone does not establish the function premise.
hints.pause: Find a candidate needing a full proof of integer-valuedness.

recall.reminder: One non-integer derivative value refutes the derivative’s universal condition.

hints.title: Prove the remaining universal claim
hints.body: Factor the candidate numerators to expose products of consecutive integers; one of two consecutive integers is even, including for negative inputs.
hints.recap: A guaranteed factor can justify division for every integer.
hints.pitfall: Finite examples do not prove an all-integers statement.
hints.pause: Prove the chosen function is always integral and combine that with a valid derivative exception.

recall.reminder: A guaranteed factor can justify division for every integer.

solution:
A fails the premise at x=0, giving 1/4. B fails it at x=1, giving 3/2.

For C, f(x)=x(x+1)(x2+1)/2 is an integer for every integer x because x(x+1) is even. But f′(0)=1/2, so C is a counterexample.

D is not: f(x)=[x(x+1)/2]2 and f′(x)=x(x+1)(2x+1)/2 are both integer-valued at integer inputs. Answer C.
knowledgePattern: Distinguish integer-valued polynomials from integer-valued derivatives
